problems.memo_sentence: The authors propose a three-part quantum option-pricing algorithm using a unary encoding where exactly one qubit in the register is in state |1⟩ per basis element: (1) a low-depth amplitude loading circuit that prepares the asset-price distribution at maturity using partial-SWAP gates whose angles encode time dependence, (2) a payoff computation step implemented with simple controlled-Ry gates that map the payoff into the probability of measuring an ancilla qubit, and (3) a standard amplitude estimation stage with a simplified oracle and reflection operator S0 constructed from only a few gates. The unary layout assumes qubits arranged on a 1D line with two-local interactions and can benefit from hardware that natively supports partial-iSWAP-like interactions.
problems.source_evidence: “The unary scheme brings further advantage since it allows for a post-selection strategy that results in error mitigation.” / “Read-out in all qubits is a requirement for post-selection to reduce errors.” / “The unary representation also provides a post-selection consistency check that allows for a substantial mitigation in the error of the computation.”
problems.explanation: The memo describes the algorithmic structure but omits the paper’s central post-selection/error-mitigation mechanism, which is part of the unary method’s claimed advantage and not just an implementation detail.

problems.memo_sentence: The unary representation is reported to substantially simplify circuit structure, yielding low and time-independent depth for distribution loading (⌊n/2⌋+1) and overall O(n) partial-SWAP and O(κn) controlled-Ry gates, as well as a simplified S0 operator in amplitude estimation.
problems.source_evidence: “the circuit will always be of depth ⌊n/2⌋ + 1” / “The unary algorithm needs O(n) partial-SWAP gates ... and O(κn) controlled-Ry gates” / “That being the case, S0 can be constructed out of 2 single-qubit gates and one entangling gate.”
problems.explanation: The depth and gate-count statements are supported, but the memo presents them as a general simplification without noting that the paper’s gate-count tables depend on the native gate set and connectivity assumptions. The simplification is conditional on the idealized architecture discussed later.

problems.memo_sentence: The authors explicitly acknowledge that unary encoding incurs linear qubit overhead, requiring linearly many qubits in the number of bins and offering lower precision than binary encoding for a fixed qubit budget.
problems.source_evidence: “the number of qubits in the unary algorithm scales linearly with the number of bins, while in the binary algorithm it is logarithmic with the target precision. This results in a worse asymptotic scaling for the unary algorithm.” / “Given a fixed number of qubits, the unary scheme allows for a lower precision than the binary one.”
problems.explanation: The memo captures the linear-qubit overhead, but it misses the paper’s explicit statement that this gives unary worse asymptotic scaling than binary. That limitation is a core caveat of the method.

problems.memo_sentence: The paper targets quantum pricing of a single-asset European-style option, motivated by the cost of classical Monte Carlo simulations for estimating expected option returns.
problems.source_evidence: Results sections report noisy-simulation findings, KL-divergence comparisons, payoff-error curves, and AE robustness; e.g., “the unary algorithm is more robust to noise” and “Amplitude Estimation reduces with every iteration the uncertainty in the value of the expected payoﬀ.”
problems.explanation: The memo’s framing leans heavily on the abstract/introduction and underrepresents the paper’s empirical findings and simulation-based conclusions. This is not wrong, but it is a noticeable bias toward setup over results.

problems.memo_sentence: The paper frames the unary algorithm as targeting an intermediate regime between today’s devices and fully fault-tolerant quantum computers and suggests several extensions, including adapting the encoding so qubits represent non-equispaced bins to increase precision and exploring extensions to multi-asset option computations.
problems.source_evidence: “The unary algorithm aims to be used during a middle stage between current quantum computers and fault-tolerant devices.” / “It is possible, for instance, to increase precision by taking the qubits to represent non equispaced elements in the probability distribution.” / “Ideas to include multi-asset computations are also available [63].”
problems.explanation: The memo is broadly accurate, but it omits that these are presented as tentative future ideas rather than developed methods. The source language is explicitly prospective and cautious.
